problem.question: Will tomorrow's AQI in this city be 'Poor' or worse (AQI >= 201)?
problem.type: Binary classification (1 = Poor or worse tomorrow, 0 = otherwise)
problem.descriptive: What happened? Average AQI per city, worst months, pollutant trends.
problem.predictive: What will happen? Probability that tomorrow's AQI crosses 200.
problem.prescriptive: What should we do? Issue a health alert, close schools, restrict trucks.
problem.industry: Public health departments, smart-city control rooms, hospitals (prepare for asthma cases), schools, air purifier / mask companies.
ethics: Location bias: Monitoring stations are concentrated in big cities, so small towns and rural areas are under-represented.
Missing data: Sensors fail more in some cities than others, so the gaps are not random and can bias the model.
Missed alerts: A false negative means vulnerable people (children, elderly, asthma patients) get no warning, so recall matters most.
Privacy: The data is city-level and public (CPCB), so no personal data is used. Linking it to individual health records would need consent and anonymisation.
False alarms: Too many wrong alerts cause panic, economic loss and alert fatigue.

data.source: Kaggle: Air Quality Data in India (2015-2020), CPCB stations

validation.method: Chronological split at 2019-07-01 + TimeSeriesSplit(5) on the training years

table.what: Too simple: cannot see today's pollution at all

table.model: Overfit: degree-3 polynomial, almost no regularization
table.what: Hundreds of feature combinations memorise the 1,500 training days

table.model: Fixed: same polynomial + strong L2 regularization (C=0.01)
table.what: Regularization shrinks the weights, so the train-test gap closes

table.model: Good fit: tuned logistic regression (full training data)

limitations: No weather data (wind speed, rain, temperature inversion) which strongly drives smog.
Many values were missing and had to be filled in, which adds uncertainty.
Stations are mostly in big cities, so results may not hold for rural areas.
The test year includes the 2020 COVID lockdown, an unusual clean-air period.
Only one day ahead; health planning often needs 3 to 7 day forecasts.
